title: Confidence Intervals
interviewAnswer: A frequentist 95% confidence interval is produced by a procedure that would contain the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. It is not literally a 95% probability statement about a fixed parameter after observing the data.
why: Confidence intervals test whether you understand uncertainty rather than reporting point estimates as if they were exact.
intuition: A point estimate gives one number; a confidence interval shows the range of values compatible with sampling uncertainty under a specified procedure. Wider intervals mean more uncertainty.
deepDive: In frequentist inference, the parameter is fixed and the interval is random before sampling. A 95% confidence procedure has 95% long-run coverage under its assumptions. Width depends on standard error, confidence level and sample size. Correct coverage can fail when assumptions, dependence, or repeated peeking are ignored.
math:
Generic form: estimate ± critical_value × standard_error
For a mean with large n: X̄ ± z_(1-α/2) σ/√n
workedExample: If a conversion lift is estimated at +1.2 percentage points with a 95% CI of [-0.2, 2.6], the data are compatible with both a small negative and a useful positive effect; the point estimate alone is not enough.
code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
x=np.array([10,11,12,9,13,12,11])
mean=x.mean(); se=stats.sem(x)
print(stats.t.interval(.95, df=len(x)-1, loc=mean, scale=se))
commonMistakes: Saying there is a 95% probability the fixed frequentist parameter lies in this observed interval.
Reporting a CI without the assumptions or sample design.
Treating a narrow but biased interval as trustworthy.

production: Confidence intervals are useful for experiment effects, model metrics, latency estimates and business KPIs. Slice-level intervals can reveal when apparent subgroup differences are mostly sampling noise.
